decks.title: Current Electricity — Part 1: Current, resistance and power
goals: Derive the relation between current and drift velocity and define mobility
Distinguish ohmic and non-ohmic conductors; use resistivity and conductivity
Explain how resistivity depends on temperature
Calculate the power dissipated in resistors

slides.heading: Current Electricity
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what happens inside a wire when current flows, why materials resist it, and how much power that resistance turns into heat.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: current, drift velocity, Ohm’s law, resistivity and temperature, power

slides.narration: Switch on a ceiling fan and the current starts almost at once, yet the electrons in the wire crawl along at less than a millimetre per second. In this part we explain that puzzle with drift velocity, derive Ohm’s law from it, see how the material and temperature decide resistance, and calculate the heating power of resistors, from a geyser element to a phone charger cable.

slides.heading: Electric current
slides.body_md:
**Current** is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section:
$$I = \dfrac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}\ \ (\text{steady}),\qquad I = \dfrac{dq}{dt},\qquad 1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C s}^{-1}$$
Its direction (conventional current) is the direction in which positive charge would flow; in metals the electrons move the other way.
bullets: Current is a scalar: it has a sense along the wire but does not add as a vector.
Charge carriers: electrons in metals, ions in electrolytes, electrons and holes in semiconductors.

visual.alt: Table of typical currents from lightning to nerve signals

slides.narration: Current measures how much charge passes a cross-section each second; one ampere is one coulomb per second. By convention its direction is the way positive charge would move, so in a metal wire the electrons actually travel opposite to the current arrow. Although we draw arrows for current, it is a scalar: at a junction currents add as plain numbers, which is the basis of Kirchhoff’s first rule.

slides.heading: Drift velocity
slides.body_md:
Free electrons move randomly at high speed, but with no field their average velocity is zero. A field $\vec E$ gives each electron an acceleration $-e\vec E/m$ between collisions. The average velocity gained is the **drift velocity**:
$$\vec v_d = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m}\,\tau$$
where $\tau$ is the average time between collisions (relaxation time).

slides.narration: Inside a metal the free electrons zip around randomly at very high speeds, colliding with ions. With no field, their velocities average to zero, so there is no current. A field nudges every electron in the direction opposite to the field between collisions. The small average velocity this produces is the drift velocity: e E over m, times the average time between collisions. It is tiny, but there are enormous numbers of electrons.

slides.heading: Current and drift velocity
slides.body_md: In time $\Delta t$, all free electrons within a length $v_d\,\Delta t$ cross a section of area $A$. With $n$ free electrons per unit volume:
bullets: Current density $j = I/A = n e v_d$.
**Mobility** $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$, unit m² V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$: drift speed per unit field.

math: \Delta q = n e A\, v_d\,\Delta t \quad\Rightarrow\quad I = n e A v_d
slides.narration: Picture a length of wire equal to the distance an electron drifts in a time delta t. Every free electron in that length crosses the end section in that time. Their number is n times A times that length, so the charge is n e A v d delta t. Dividing by time gives I equals n e A v d. Mobility is the drift speed for each volt per metre of field, and equals e tau over m.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how slow is the drift?
slides.body_md: A copper wire of cross-section $1.0$ mm² carries $2.0$ A. Copper has $n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}$ free electrons per m³. Find the drift speed.
bullets: Step 1 — $A = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m².
Step 2 — $v_d = \dfrac{I}{n e A} = \dfrac{2.0}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$.
Step 3 — at this speed an electron takes about 1.9 hours to drift one metre.
Why lights come on at once — the field travels along the wire at nearly the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start drifting together.

visual.alt: Worked table: electron density, area and a drift speed of about 0.15 millimetre per second

slides.narration: Convert one square millimetre to ten to the minus six square metre, then divide the current by n e A. The drift speed is about one point five times ten to the minus four metre per second, roughly a seventh of a millimetre each second. An electron would need about two hours to drift one metre. Lights still come on instantly because the field is set up along the whole wire almost immediately.

slides.heading: Quick check: drift and area
slides.body_md: The same current flows through a thick and a thin section of one copper wire.
slides.narration: The current and the electron density are the same in both sections. Use I equals n e A v d to compare the drift speeds.

slides.heading: Ohm’s law, resistance and resistivity
slides.body_md:
From $v_d = e E\tau/m$ and $E = V/l$: $I = n e A v_d = \dfrac{n e^2\tau A}{ml}V$, so $V = IR$ with
$$R = \rho\,\dfrac{l}{A},\qquad \rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau},\qquad \sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho}$$
bullets: $R$ depends on the sample (length, area); $\rho$ depends only on the material and its temperature.
Units: $R$ in ohm (Ω), $\rho$ in Ω m, conductivity $\sigma$ in S m$^{-1}$.
Vector form: $\vec j = \sigma\vec E$.

visual.alt: Table of approximate resistivities: copper, nichrome, pure silicon and glass, from conductors to insulators

slides.narration: Put the drift velocity into I equals n e A v d and use E equals V over l. The current comes out proportional to the voltage, which is Ohm’s law, with resistance rho l over A. Resistivity, rho, belongs to the material: it is m over n e squared tau. A long thin wire has more resistance than a short thick one of the same metal. Conductivity is just one over resistivity.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: resistance from resistivity
slides.body_md: (a) Find the resistance of 50 m of copper wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² ($\rho = 1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω m). (b) A copper coil has resistance 10.0 Ω at 20 °C. Find its resistance at 100 °C ($\alpha = 3.9 \times 10^{-3}$ °C$^{-1}$).
bullets: (a) $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times 50}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.85$ Ω.
Check — a 31% rise for an 80 °C rise is typical of metals.

slides.heading: Linear and non-linear V–I characteristics
slides.body_md: Ohm’s law is not a law of nature; many devices do not obey it.
columns:
**Ohmic (linear)**

- $I$ proportional to $V$: a straight line through the origin.
- Same $R$ for every current and for both directions.
- Example: a metal wire at constant temperature.

**Non-ohmic (non-linear)**

- $V$ not proportional to $I$ (filament lamp, as it heats).
- Depends on the sign of $V$ (a diode conducts one way).
- More than one $V$ for the same $I$ (GaAs devices).

functions.label: ohmic resistor (R = 5 Ω): straight line through the origin
filament lamp: curve bends over as it heats

visual.alt: Current against voltage: a straight line through the origin for an ohmic resistor and a curve that bends towards the voltage axis for a filament lamp whose resistance rises as it heats
visual.caption: Ohmic: constant slope 1/R. Non-ohmic: slope changes with V.

slides.narration: For an ohmic conductor the graph of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin, and reversing the voltage simply reverses the current. Many devices break this rule. A lamp filament heats up, so its resistance rises and the graph bends. A diode lets current through in one direction only. Some materials, such as gallium arsenide, even have regions where the current falls as voltage rises.

slides.heading: Resistivity and temperature
slides.body_md: For metals over a moderate range: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, with $\alpha > 0$.
bullets: **Metals:** hotter ions vibrate more, so $\tau$ falls and $\rho$ rises.
**Alloys** (nichrome, manganin, constantan): very small $\alpha$, used for standard resistors and heater elements.
**Semiconductors:** $n$ rises sharply with temperature, so $\rho$ falls ($\alpha < 0$).

visual.alt: Relative resistivity against temperature: copper rises steadily, nichrome barely changes and a semiconductor falls steeply
visual.caption: Shapes only; the semiconductor curve is scaled to fit.

slides.narration: In a metal, heating makes the ions vibrate more strongly, so electrons collide more often; tau falls and resistivity rises almost linearly. Alloys such as manganin hardly change, which makes them ideal for standard resistors. In a semiconductor, heating frees many more charge carriers, so n grows faster than tau falls, and the resistivity drops steeply. The temperature coefficient is then negative.

slides.heading: Quick check: semiconductor heating
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason.
slides.narration: Think about what happens to the number of charge carriers and to the time between collisions when a semiconductor is heated.

slides.heading: Electrical energy and power
slides.body_md:
Charge $q$ falling through potential difference $V$ loses energy $qV$, which appears as heat in a resistor. Power:
$$P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R},\qquad \text{energy } W = Pt$$
bullets: Use $I^2R$ when the current is the same (series), $V^2/R$ when the voltage is the same (parallel).
Commercial unit: 1 kWh $= 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J.
Transmission at high voltage cuts the $I^2R$ loss in the cables.

visual.alt: Table: in series the larger resistor dissipates more power; in parallel the smaller one does

slides.narration: Each coulomb passing through a resistor loses V joules, so the power is V times I. Using Ohm’s law this becomes I squared R or V squared over R. Pick the form that matches what is fixed: in series the current is common, so the larger resistance gets hotter; in parallel the voltage is common, so the smaller resistance gets hotter. This is also why power lines use very high voltages.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a heater on a low supply
slides.body_md: A heater is rated 1000 W, 220 V. Find (a) its resistance and rated current, (b) its power if the supply falls to 200 V (resistance unchanged).
bullets: Check — a 9% drop in voltage gives about a 17% drop in power, because $P \propto V^2$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 1000 watts at 220 volts and about 826 watts at 200 volts

slides.narration: Use the rating to find the resistance: two hundred and twenty squared over one thousand gives forty eight point four ohms, and the rated current is about four and a half amperes. When the supply sags to two hundred volts, the resistance stays the same, so the power is two hundred squared over forty eight point four, about eight hundred and twenty six watts. Power falls faster than voltage because it depends on V squared.

slides.heading: Quick check: bulbs in series
slides.body_md: Two bulbs, 100 W and 60 W (both rated 220 V), are joined in series across 220 V.

functions.label: ohmic resistor (R = 5 Ω): straight line through the origin
filament lamp: curve bends over as it heats

visual.alt: Current against voltage: a straight line through the origin for an ohmic resistor and a curve that bends towards the voltage axis for a filament lamp whose resistance rises as it heats
visual.caption: Ohmic: constant slope 1/R. Non-ohmic: slope changes with V.

slides.narration: Find which bulb has the larger resistance from P equals V squared over R. In series the current is the same, so use I squared R.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

visual.alt: Summary table of current, drift, mobility, resistance, temperature dependence and power

slides.narration: To sum up: current is charge per second and equals n e A v d. Electrons drift slowly, with a speed set by the field and the time between collisions. Resistance is rho l over A, and resistivity depends on the material and temperature, rising for metals and falling for semiconductors. Some devices are not ohmic. Power in a resistor is V I, I squared R or V squared over R.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Derivation of $I = n e A v_d$: draw the cylinder of length $v_d\Delta t$, count the electrons, divide by $\Delta t$.
Stretching a wire to $k$ times its length (same volume): area falls $k$ times, so $R$ rises $k^2$ times.
Do not confuse drift speed (about $10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$) with the speed of the signal (close to the speed of light).
Rated power and voltage give $R$; then use the actual voltage.

visual.alt: Table of how resistance changes when a wire is lengthened, thickened or stretched

slides.narration: Examiners love the drift-velocity derivation: draw the cylinder, count electrons and divide by time. For stretched wires remember the volume stays the same, so doubling the length halves the area and the resistance becomes four times. Keep the drift speed and the signal speed separate in your mind. And for appliances, find the resistance from the rating first, then apply the actual voltage.

decks.title: Current Electricity — Part 2: Cells, Kirchhoff’s rules and bridges
goals: Relate the terminal voltage of a cell to its emf and internal resistance
Combine cells in series and in parallel
Apply Kirchhoff’s junction and loop rules to multi-loop circuits
Derive the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge and use a metre bridge

slides.heading: Cells, Kirchhoff’s rules and bridges
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what a cell really supplies, how to solve any network of cells and resistors, and how a balanced bridge measures resistance precisely.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: emf and internal resistance, combinations of cells, Kirchhoff’s rules, Wheatstone bridge, metre bridge

slides.narration: Why does a car’s headlight dim when the starter motor runs? Because every real cell has internal resistance. In this part we model a cell by its emf and internal resistance, combine cells, and learn two rules from Kirchhoff that solve any circuit. Finally we use them to find when a Wheatstone bridge is balanced, the principle of the metre bridge you use in the laboratory.

slides.heading: EMF and internal resistance
slides.body_md: The **emf** $E$ of a cell is the potential difference between its terminals when **no current** flows (the work done per unit charge by the cell’s chemical action). With current $I$ through internal resistance $r$:
bullets: Discharging: $V < E$. Charging (current forced in at the + terminal): $V = E + Ir$.
Short circuit ($R = 0$): $I_\text{max} = E/r$.

slides.narration: A cell drives charge round a circuit using chemical energy. Its emf is the voltage across its terminals when it supplies no current. Real cells have internal resistance, so when a current flows, part of the emf is used up inside the cell, I r, and the terminal voltage falls to E minus I r. While a cell is being charged the current flows the other way and the terminal voltage is E plus I r.

slides.heading: Terminal voltage against current
slides.body_md: Plotting $V$ against $I$ for one cell with different loads gives a straight line: intercept $E$, slope $-r$.

functions.label: V = E − Ir (E = 12 V, r = 0.5 Ω)

visual.alt: Terminal voltage falls linearly with current from 12 volts at zero current to zero at the short-circuit current of 24 amperes; the slope is minus r
visual.caption: Intercept on the V-axis = E; slope = −r.

slides.narration: If you connect different loads to the same cell and plot terminal voltage against current, you get a falling straight line. Where the current is zero, the voltage equals the emf. Its slope is minus the internal resistance. Extend it to zero voltage and you find the short-circuit current, E over r. This graph is how internal resistance is measured in the laboratory.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a cell under load
slides.body_md: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω resistor. Find the current, the terminal voltage, and the current if the terminals are shorted.
bullets: Step 2 — $V = E - Ir = 12 - 2.0 \times 0.5 = 11.0$ V (also $IR = 2.0 \times 5.5 = 11$ V).
Step 3 — short circuit: $I = E/r = 12/0.5 = 24$ A — large enough to overheat the cell.

functions.label: V = E − Ir (E = 12 V, r = 0.5 Ω)

visual.alt: Terminal voltage falls linearly with current from 12 volts at zero current to zero at the short-circuit current of 24 amperes; the slope is minus r
visual.caption: Intercept on the V-axis = E; slope = −r.

slides.narration: The total resistance is the external five point five ohms plus the internal half ohm, so the current is two amperes. One volt is lost inside the cell, leaving eleven volts at the terminals, which matches I times R. If the terminals were shorted, only the internal resistance would limit the current, giving twenty four amperes. That is why shorting a battery can make it dangerously hot.

slides.heading: Cells in series and in parallel
slides.body_md: Combining cells (all connected the same way round):
columns:
**Series** (+ of one to − of the next)
$$E_\text{eq} = E_1 + E_2 + \dots,\qquad r_\text{eq} = r_1 + r_2 + \dots$$
A cell connected the wrong way round subtracts its emf.

**Parallel** (+ to +, − to −)
$$\dfrac{E_\text{eq}}{r_\text{eq}} = \dfrac{E_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2}{r_2},\qquad \dfrac{1}{r_\text{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}$$
$n$ identical cells: emf $E$, internal resistance $r/n$.

slides.heading: Kirchhoff’s rules
slides.body_md: Two rules solve any network:
bullets: **Junction rule** (conservation of charge): at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving, $\sum I = 0$.
**Loop rule** (conservation of energy): round any closed loop, the algebraic sum of potential changes is zero, $\sum \Delta V = 0$.
Signs: going through a resistor **along** the assumed current, potential drops by IR; going through a cell from − to +, potential rises by E.
If a current comes out negative, it simply flows opposite to the arrow you assumed.

slides.narration: Kirchhoff’s first rule says charge cannot pile up at a junction, so the currents flowing in equal the currents flowing out. The second rule says that if you walk round any closed loop and add up every rise and fall of potential, you return to where you started, so the total is zero. Choose current directions, apply the sign rules carefully, and a negative answer just means the true current flows the other way.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a two-loop circuit
slides.body_md: In the circuit, $E_1 = 12$ V with $R_1 = 2$ Ω, $E_2 = 6$ V with $R_2 = 2$ Ω, and $R_3 = 4$ Ω joins A and B. Find all three currents.
bullets: Step 1 — junction A: $I_1 + I_2 = I_3$ (all assumed flowing up the cell branches into A).
Step 2 — left loop: $12 - 2I_1 - 4I_3 = 0$; right loop: $6 - 2I_2 - 4I_3 = 0$.
Meaning — $I_2$ is negative: 0.6 A flows **down** through the 6 V cell, charging it.

Adjust one resistor until the galvanometer shows no deflection. Then points B and D are at the same potential, and the ratio P over Q equals R over S. slides.heading: Deriving the balance condition
slides.body_md: With zero current in the galvanometer ($I_g = 0$), apply Kirchhoff’s rules:
bullets: Junctions B and D: the current $I_1$ in P also flows through Q; the current $I_2$ in R also flows through S.
Loop A–B–D–A: $-I_1P + I_2R = 0$ (no drop across G), so $I_1P = I_2R$.
Loop B–C–D–B: $-I_1Q + I_2S = 0$, so $I_1Q = I_2S$.
Divide: $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the metre bridge
slides.body_md: In a metre bridge, an unknown resistance X is in the left gap and a 4.0 Ω resistor in the right gap. The balance point is 40.0 cm from the left end. Find X.
bullets: Step 1 — the wire segments act as R and S, proportional to their lengths: $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$.
Step 2 — $X = 4.0 \times \dfrac{40}{60} = 2.67$ Ω.
Check — X is smaller than 4 Ω, consistent with balance on the shorter side.
Good practice — choose R so that balance is near the middle of the wire, to reduce end errors.

slides.narration: A metre bridge is a Wheatstone bridge in which two of the arms are parts of a uniform one metre wire. Their resistances are proportional to their lengths, so X over R equals l over one hundred minus l. With balance at forty centimetres, X is four times forty over sixty, about two point six seven ohms. Balance near the middle of the wire gives the most accurate result.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: $\sum I = 0$ at a junction; $\sum \Delta V = 0$ round a loop

visual.alt: Summary table of terminal voltage, current, cell combinations, Kirchhoff’s rules and bridge balance conditions

slides.narration: To sum up: a cell has an emf and an internal resistance, so its terminal voltage drops as it supplies more current. Cells in series add their emfs and resistances; identical cells in parallel keep the emf but share the internal resistance. Kirchhoff’s junction and loop rules come from conservation of charge and energy, and they give the Wheatstone balance condition, P over Q equals R over S, used in the metre bridge.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Mark assumed current directions on the circuit before writing any equation; keep them fixed.
Loop signs: resistor along current −IR; cell from − to + is +E.
A negative answer is not wrong: the current flows the other way.
Bridge balance does not depend on the cell’s emf or on the galvanometer’s resistance.

visual.alt: Table of sign rules for the loop rule: resistors along and against the current and cells in each direction

slides.narration: In circuit questions, draw and label your current directions first and stick to them. Use the sign table for every element you pass through. If an answer comes out negative, keep it: it just tells you the direction. Remember that at balance a Wheatstone bridge does not care about the emf or the galvanometer, which is why the method is accurate.

sections.heading: 1. Current, drift velocity and mobility
sections.body_md:
**Current** $I = dq/dt$ (ampere, A = C s$^{-1}$); conventional direction = direction of positive-charge flow. In metals, electrons move opposite to it.

**Drift velocity.** Free electrons move randomly (no net velocity without a field). In a field each gains $-e\vec E/m$ between collisions; averaged over the relaxation time $\tau$:
$$\vec v_d = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m}\tau$$

**Current–drift relation.** In time $\Delta t$ the electrons in a length $v_d\Delta t$ cross area $A$: $\Delta q = n e A v_d\Delta t$, so
$$I = n e A v_d,\qquad j = \dfrac{I}{A} = n e v_d$$

**Mobility** $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$ (m² V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$).

Typical drift speed: about $10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$; the field (and so the signal) travels at nearly the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights at once.

key_terms.definition_md: Average velocity of free electrons in a conductor in an electric field.
Average time between successive collisions of a free electron.
Drift speed per unit electric field.

sections.heading: 2. Ohm’s law, resistivity and conductivity
sections.body_md:
Substituting $v_d = eE\tau/m$ and $E = V/l$ into $I = n e A v_d$:
$$V = IR,\qquad R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A},\qquad \rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau},\qquad \sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho},\qquad \vec j = \sigma\vec E$$

- $R$ (ohm) depends on the sample; $\rho$ (Ω m) only on the material and temperature.
- Stretching a wire $k$ times (constant volume): $R \to k^2R$.

**V–I characteristics.** *Linear (ohmic):* straight line through the origin, same for both directions. *Non-linear:* filament lamp (R rises as it heats), diode (depends on the sign of V), GaAs (more than one V for some I).

**Temperature dependence.**
- Metals: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, $\alpha > 0$ — hotter ions, more collisions, smaller $\tau$.
- Alloys (nichrome, manganin, constantan): very small $\alpha$ — standard resistors and heater elements.
- Semiconductors: $\rho$ falls with temperature ($\alpha < 0$) because $n$ rises steeply.

key_terms.definition_md: Resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross-section; a property of the material.
A conductor whose current is proportional to the applied voltage at constant temperature.
Fractional change in resistivity per degree rise in temperature, α.

sections.heading: 3. Electrical energy and power
sections.body_md:
Charge $q$ moving through potential difference $V$ transfers energy $qV$. Power delivered to a resistor:
$$P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$$

- Series (same $I$): the larger $R$ dissipates more ($I^2R$).
- Parallel (same $V$): the smaller $R$ dissipates more ($V^2/R$).
- Rated values give $R = V_\text{rated}^2/P_\text{rated}$; then use the actual voltage.
- Energy $W = Pt$; 1 kWh $= 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J.
- Power is sent over long distances at high voltage so that the current, and the $I^2R$ loss in the lines, is small.

key_terms.definition_md: Energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour, $3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J.

sections.heading: 4. Cells: emf, internal resistance and combinations
sections.body_md:
**EMF** $E$: terminal p.d. of a cell when it supplies no current. **Internal resistance** $r$: resistance of the electrolyte and electrodes.

- Discharging: $V = E - Ir$, $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}$. Charging: $V = E + Ir$.
- Short circuit: $I = E/r$. Open circuit: $V = E$.
- $V$–$I$ graph: straight line, intercept $E$, slope $-r$.

**Combinations**
- Series: $E_\text{eq} = \sum E_i$ (a reversed cell subtracts), $r_\text{eq} = \sum r_i$.
- Parallel: $\dfrac{E_\text{eq}}{r_\text{eq}} = \sum \dfrac{E_i}{r_i}$, $\dfrac{1}{r_\text{eq}} = \sum \dfrac{1}{r_i}$. For $n$ identical cells: $E$, $r/n$.

key_terms.definition_md: Work done by the source per unit charge in taking charge round the circuit; equals the terminal p.d. on open circuit.
Resistance offered by the cell itself to the current through it.

sections.heading: 5. Kirchhoff’s rules
sections.body_md:
**Junction rule** (charge conservation): $\sum I_\text{in} = \sum I_\text{out}$ at every junction.

**Loop rule** (energy conservation): $\sum \Delta V = 0$ round any closed loop.

**Method:** (1) mark a current in every branch with an assumed direction; (2) apply the junction rule to reduce unknowns; (3) choose independent loops and add potential changes with the sign rules (resistor along I: $-IR$; cell − to +: $+E$); (4) solve; a negative current flows opposite to the arrow.

*Worked result (deck example):* 12 V/2 Ω and 6 V/2 Ω branches with 4 Ω across them give 2.4 A, −0.6 A (the 6 V cell is charged) and 1.8 A.

key_terms.definition_md: The algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero.
The algebraic sum of potential changes round a closed loop is zero.

sections.heading: 6. Wheatstone bridge and metre bridge
sections.body_md:
Arms P (A–B), Q (B–C), R (A–D), S (D–C); cell across A–C, galvanometer across B–D.

**Balance** ($I_g = 0$): B and D at the same potential. Loop ABDA: $I_1P = I_2R$; loop BCDB: $I_1Q = I_2S$. Dividing:
$$\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$$
Balance is independent of the emf and of the galvanometer’s resistance; the cell and galvanometer may be interchanged.

**Metre bridge:** two arms are lengths $l$ and $100 - l$ (cm) of a uniform wire: $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$ (X in the left gap). Best accuracy with balance near the middle; end errors are reduced by interchanging X and R and averaging.

questions.stem_md: A copper wire has a thick section of cross-section $2A$ joined to a thin section of cross-section $A$, and carries a steady current. Compared with the thick section, the drift speed in the thin section is
questions.solution_md: $I = n e A v_d$ with the same $I$ and $n$: $v_d \propto 1/A$, so halving the area doubles $v_d$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A wire of cross-section 2.0 mm² carries 3.0 A. The free-electron density is 8.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Find the drift speed, in mm s⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: v_d = I/(n e A) ≈ 0.117 mm s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of mobility of charge carriers is
questions.solution_md: Mobility is drift speed per unit field: (m s$^{-1}$)/(V m$^{-1}$) = m² V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Copper has resistivity 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m and 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. Estimate the relaxation time of its electrons, in femtoseconds (1 fs = 10⁻¹⁵ s). (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
The potential difference across a metal wire is doubled, its temperature staying the same. The drift speed of its electrons
questions.solution_md: $E = V/l$ doubles, and $v_d = eE\tau/m$ is proportional to $E$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A fixed potential difference is applied across a wire. If the wire is replaced by one of the same material and thickness but twice as long, the drift speed
questions.solution_md: The field $E = V/l$ halves, so $v_d = eE\tau/m$ halves. (The current also halves, consistent with $I = n e A v_d$.) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The drift speed of free electrons in a current-carrying copper wire is close to the speed of light.
questions.solution_md: False. Drift speeds are about $10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$. It is the electric field (the signal) that travels at nearly the speed of light.

questions.stem_md: In a metal wire, the direction of conventional current is opposite to the direction of motion of the ___.
questions.solution_md: Of the free **electrons**, which carry negative charge.

questions.stem_md: Electrons in a wire drift at only about 0.1 mm s⁻¹, yet a lamp several metres from the switch lights almost instantly. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Closing the switch sets up an **electric field** along the whole wire almost at the **speed of light**. Free electrons are already present **everywhere** in the wire, including the lamp filament, so they all start drifting **at once**. No electron has to travel from the switch to the lamp.

questions.solution_md: Separate the speed of the field from the drift speed of electrons.

marking_scheme.step: Field established along the wire almost at the speed of light

questions.stem_md: Derive the relation $I = n e A v_d$ between the current in a conductor and the drift velocity of its electrons. Hence define current density.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the conductor have cross-section $A$ and $n$ free electrons per unit volume, each drifting with speed $v_d$. In time $\Delta t$ each electron moves $v_d\Delta t$, so all electrons within a length $v_d\Delta t$ behind a cross-section cross it. Their number is $nAv_d\Delta t$ and their charge is $\Delta q = n e A v_d\Delta t$. Hence $I = \dfrac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = n e A v_d$. **Current density** is current per unit area normal to the flow: $j = I/A = n e v_d$ (A m$^{-2}$).

questions.solution_md: Count the electrons in a cylinder of length v_d Δt.

marking_scheme.step: Cylinder of length v_d Δt and number nAv_dΔt
Charge and I = n e A v_d

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The drift velocity of free electrons in a metal is very small compared with their random thermal speeds.

**Reason (R):** Free electrons in a metal do not move at all between collisions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: electrons move very fast between collisions, but in random directions; the field only adds a small average drift — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Wires P and Q are of the same metal and the same length, at the same temperature. On a graph of current (y-axis) against voltage (x-axis), the line for P is steeper than the line for Q. Which is correct?

options.text_md: P and Q have the same thickness

questions.solution_md: A steeper I–V line means a larger $1/R$, so P has the smaller resistance. With the same $\rho$ and $l$, $R = \rho l/A$ is smaller for the larger area: P is thicker — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A wire of resistance 2 Ω is stretched uniformly to three times its length. Its new resistance is
questions.solution_md: Volume is constant, so $A$ falls to $A/3$ while $l$ becomes $3l$: $R = \rho l/A$ rises $9$ times, $2 \times 9 = 18$ Ω — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm ___.
questions.solution_md: Ohm **metre** (Ω m), from $\rho = RA/l$.

questions.stem_md: A nichrome wire is 2.0 m long with a cross-section of 0.50 mm². Nichrome has resistivity 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Find its resistance, in ohms.
questions.solution_md: $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.0}{0.50 \times 10^{-6}} = 4.0$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: A copper coil has a resistance of 20.0 Ω at 20 °C. At what temperature will its resistance be 24.0 Ω? Take α = 4.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Give the answer in °C.

marking_scheme.step: Correct use of R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The resistance of a pure semiconductor decreases when it is heated.

**Reason (R):** Heating increases the number of charge carriers in a semiconductor far more than it reduces the time between collisions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; with $\rho = m/n e^2\tau$, the large rise in $n$ outweighs the fall in $\tau$, which explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the graph of current against voltage is

options.text_md: a straight line that cuts the current axis above the origin
a straight line through the origin
a curve bending towards the voltage axis

questions.solution_md: Ohmic means $I \propto V$: a straight line through the origin with slope $1/R$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The current–voltage graph of a filament lamp bends towards the voltage axis at higher voltages because

options.text_md: the filament gets hotter, so its resistance decreases
the lamp obeys Ohm’s law exactly
the filament gets hotter, so its resistance increases
the number of free electrons in the filament falls to zero

questions.solution_md: A hotter metal filament has larger resistivity, so each extra volt gives less extra current — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Standard resistance coils are usually made of manganin because it has

options.text_md: a very small temperature coefficient of resistivity
a negative temperature coefficient like a semiconductor

questions.solution_md: Its resistance hardly changes with temperature, so the coil keeps its value — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The resistivity of a metal increases with temperature.

**Reason (R):** The number of free electrons per unit volume in a metal increases greatly with temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: $n$ is nearly constant in a metal; the rise in $\rho$ comes from more frequent collisions (smaller $\tau$) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Ohm’s law holds for every conductor under all conditions.
questions.solution_md: False. Filament lamps, diodes and many semiconductor devices are non-ohmic; even a metal obeys it only at constant temperature.

questions.stem_md: Match each device in Column A with the feature of its V–I characteristic in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Large current for one polarity only
Slope falls as the voltage rises
More than one voltage for the same current

questions.solution_md: Resistor → straight line (1 → s); lamp → falling slope (2 → q); diode → one polarity (3 → p); GaAs → more than one V for an I (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: I–V graphs of the same metal wire are drawn at two temperatures, T₁ and T₂. The graph at T₁ is steeper. Which is correct?
questions.solution_md: On an I–V graph the slope is $1/R$. Steeper means smaller $R$, and a metal has smaller $R$ at lower temperature — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between linear and non-linear V–I characteristics, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **linear** characteristic the current is proportional to the voltage: the graph is a straight line through the origin, the same in both directions (a metal wire at constant temperature). In a **non-linear** one, $I$ is not proportional to $V$ or depends on its sign: a filament lamp curves as it heats; a diode conducts only one way.

questions.solution_md: Contrast proportional and non-proportional behaviour with examples.

marking_scheme.step: Linear: straight line through origin, example
Non-linear: curve or polarity dependence, example

questions.stem_md: Using $\rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$, explain why the resistivity of a metal increases with temperature, while that of a semiconductor decreases.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **metal**, $n$ is large and almost **independent** of temperature. Heating makes the ions vibrate more, so electrons collide **more often** and $\tau$ **decreases**: $\rho$ rises. In a **semiconductor**, heating frees many more electrons (and holes), so $n$ **increases sharply**. Although $\tau$ also decreases, the rise in $n$ dominates, so $\rho$ **falls**.

questions.solution_md: Track n and τ separately for each material.

marking_scheme.step: So ρ of a metal increases
Semiconductor: n rises much more, ρ decreases

questions.stem_md: A room circuit on a 220 V supply is protected by a 5 A fuse. What is the largest number of 100 W bulbs that can be switched on together without blowing the fuse?
questions.solution_md: The fuse allows at most $P = VI = 220 \times 5 = 1100$ W, i.e. $1100/100 = 11$ bulbs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two identical heaters, each rated 1000 W at 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The total power drawn is
Bulbs rated 100 W, 220 V and 60 W, 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which bulb glows brighter?
questions.solution_md: $R = V^2/P$: the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance ($807$ Ω vs $484$ Ω). In series the current is the same, so $P = I^2R$ is larger for the 60 W bulb — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Find the total power dissipated, in watts.
questions.solution_md: Each has 12 V across it: $\dfrac{12^2}{4} = 36$ W and $\dfrac{12^2}{6} = 24$ W. Total $= 36 + 24 = 60$ W.

questions.stem_md: A 1.5 kW geyser is used for 2 hours every day. How many kilowatt hours (units) does it use in 30 days?
questions.solution_md: $E = Pt = 1.5 \times 2 \times 30 = 90$ kWh.

questions.stem_md: The coil of a heater is cut to half its length and the remaining half is used on the same supply voltage. The heater’s power
questions.solution_md: $R$ halves, and $P = V^2/R$ at fixed $V$ doubles — option (d). (The coil runs much hotter.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? Of two resistors connected in parallel across a supply, the one with the smaller resistance dissipates more power.
questions.solution_md: True. Both have the same voltage, and $P = V^2/R$ is larger for the smaller $R$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A 100 W, 220 V bulb has a larger resistance than a 60 W, 220 V bulb.

**Reason (R):** For appliances rated at the same voltage, $P = V^2/R$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: from $R = V^2/P$, the 100 W bulb has the smaller resistance (484 Ω against 807 Ω) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A power station sends 100 kW to a village through lines of total resistance 5.0 Ω. Find the power lost in the lines if the power is sent (a) at 1.0 kV, (b) at 10 kV. What do you conclude?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I = P/V = 100\,000/1000 = 100$ A; loss $= I^2R = 100^2 \times 5.0 = 50000$ W (half the power!).
(b) $I = 100\,000/10\,000 = 10$ A; loss $= 10^2 \times 5.0 = 500$ W.
**Conclusion:** raising the voltage 10 times cuts the current 10 times and the line loss 100 times, so power is transmitted at high voltage.

questions.solution_md: Find I = P/V, then I²R for each voltage.

marking_scheme.step: Conclusion: high voltage reduces I²R loss

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why nichrome, rather than copper, is used for the heating element of an electric iron.

answer.model_answer_md: Nichrome has a much **higher resistivity**, so a short, convenient length gives the resistance needed for the required heating. It also has a **high melting point** and does **not oxidise** easily when red-hot, whereas copper would need a very long wire and would oxidise.

questions.solution_md: Compare resistivity and behaviour at high temperature.

marking_scheme.step: High melting point / does not oxidise when hot

questions.stem_md: A student measures the resistance of a 60 W, 220 V bulb with a multimeter at room temperature and finds about 70 Ω, not the 807 Ω given by $V^2/P$. She concludes the bulb is faulty. Evaluate her conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: Her conclusion is **wrong**. $V^2/P$ gives the resistance of the filament when it is **white-hot** (about 2500 °C). Tungsten’s resistivity rises strongly with temperature, so the **cold** filament has a much **smaller** resistance. A reading of about one tenth of the hot value is normal for a working bulb.

questions.solution_md: Relate the rated resistance to the operating temperature.

marking_scheme.step: Resistance of a cold metal filament is much lower; bulb not faulty

questions.stem_md: A high-resistance voltmeter across a cell reads 1.5 V. When a 4.0 Ω resistor is connected across the cell, the reading falls to 1.2 V. The internal resistance of the cell is
Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 2.0 Ω, are connected in parallel. Find the internal resistance of the combination, in ohms.
questions.solution_md: For $n$ identical cells in parallel, $r_\text{eq} = r/n = 2.0/4 = 0.5$ Ω (emf stays 1.5 V).

questions.stem_md: A cell of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. The terminal voltage is
A battery of emf 10 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is being charged with a current of 2.0 A. The potential difference across its terminals is
questions.solution_md: While charging, current enters at the positive terminal: $V = E + Ir = 10 + 2.0 \times 1.0 = 12$ V — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A cell’s terminal voltage is 1.4 V when it supplies 0.20 A and 1.1 V when it supplies 0.80 A. Find its internal resistance and emf. Enter the emf, in volts.

marking_scheme.step: r = 0.50 Ω from the change in V and I

questions.stem_md: Four cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.10 Ω, are connected in series, but one of them is put in the wrong way round. The combination has

options.text_md: emf 3.0 V and internal resistance 0.40 Ω
emf 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.40 Ω
emf 3.0 V and internal resistance 0.20 Ω
emf 4.5 V and internal resistance 0.30 Ω

questions.solution_md: The reversed cell subtracts its emf: $1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 - 1.5 = 3.0$ V. Internal resistances always add: $4 \times 0.10 = 0.40$ Ω — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A cell of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected in parallel (positive to positive) with a cell of emf 1.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω. The equivalent emf and internal resistance are
True or false? The potential difference across the terminals of a cell can be greater than its emf.
questions.solution_md: True. When the cell is being charged, current enters at its positive terminal and $V = E + Ir > E$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The terminal voltage of a cell supplying current is less than its emf.

**Reason (R):** Part of the emf is used to drive the current through the internal resistance of the cell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; the "lost volts" $Ir$ inside the cell are exactly why $V = E - Ir < E$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two identical cells, each of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are to drive current through an external resistance $R$. Find the current when they are joined (a) in series, (b) in parallel. Show that the series arrangement gives more current when $R > r$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Series: emf $2E$, resistance $2r$: $I_s = \dfrac{2E}{R + 2r}$.
(b) Parallel: emf $E$, resistance $r/2$: $I_p = \dfrac{E}{R + r/2} = \dfrac{2E}{2R + r}$.
$I_s > I_p$ when $R + 2r < 2R + r$, that is when $R > r$. (For $R < r$ the parallel arrangement is better; for $R = r$ they are equal.)

questions.solution_md: Write both currents with the same numerator 2E and compare denominators.

questions.stem_md: In part of a circuit, a current of 1.0 A flows from point A through a 2.0 Ω resistor and then through a 3.0 V cell (entering at its negative terminal) to point B. The potential difference $V_A - V_B$ is
questions.solution_md: From A to B: across the resistor along the current the potential falls by $1.0 \times 2.0 = 2$ V; through the cell from − to + it rises by 3.0 V. So $V_B = V_A - 2 + 3$, giving $V_A - V_B = -1$ V — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Four wires meet at a junction. Currents of 3.0 A and 2.0 A flow into it along two wires, and 4.0 A flows out along the third. Find the current in the fourth wire, in amperes (it flows out of the junction).
questions.solution_md: Junction rule: in $=$ out, $3.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 + I$, so $I = 3.0 + 2.0 - 4.0 = 1$ A, flowing out.

questions.stem_md: Two branches are joined between points A and B: one has a 10 V cell in series with 1.0 Ω, the other a 5.0 V cell in series with 1.0 Ω (both cells with their positive terminals towards A, internal resistances included in these values). A 2.0 Ω resistor is also connected between A and B. Find the current in the 2.0 Ω resistor, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: Let $V_A - V_B = V$. Junction A: $\dfrac{10 - V}{1} + \dfrac{5 - V}{1} = \dfrac{V}{2}$, so $15 = 2.5V$ and $V = 6.0$ V. Current in the 2.0 Ω resistor $= V/2 = 3.0$ A (the cell currents are 4.0 A and -1.0 A).

marking_scheme.step: Junction and loop equations set up

questions.stem_md: When applying Kirchhoff’s loop rule, you move through a resistor $R$ in the direction OPPOSITE to the current $I$ in it. The potential change you write is
questions.solution_md: Current flows from higher to lower potential through a resistor, so going against it you climb by $IR$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Kirchhoff’s junction rule is a statement of the conservation of
questions.solution_md: Charge cannot accumulate at a junction in a steady state — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Kirchhoff’s loop rule is a consequence of the conservation of energy.

**Reason (R):** The electrostatic force is conservative, so the net work done on a charge taken round a closed loop is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; because the work round a closed path is zero, the potential changes round any loop must add to zero — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State Kirchhoff’s two rules for electric circuits and the conservation law on which each is based.

answer.model_answer_md: **Junction rule:** at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving — **conservation of charge**. **Loop rule:** the algebraic sum of the changes in potential round any closed loop is zero — **conservation of energy**.

questions.solution_md: State each rule with its basis.

questions.stem_md: A 9.0 V cell and a 3.0 V cell (negligible internal resistances) are connected in series with a 2.0 Ω and a 4.0 Ω resistor, with the cells OPPOSING each other. Use the loop rule to find the current and the potential difference across the 4.0 Ω resistor. Which cell is being charged?

answer.model_answer_md: Take the current in the direction driven by the 9.0 V cell. Loop rule: $9.0 - 3.0 - 2.0I - 4.0I = 0$, so $I = \dfrac{6.0}{6.0} = 1$ A. P.d. across 4.0 Ω $= 1 \times 4.0 = 4$ V. The current enters the **3.0 V cell at its positive terminal**, so the **3.0 V cell is being charged**.

questions.solution_md: Write the loop equation with opposing emfs.

questions.stem_md: In a metre bridge, the balance point is 40 cm from the left end. The resistors in the two gaps are now interchanged. The new balance point is
questions.solution_md: Before: $X/R = 40/60$. After swapping, $R/X = l/(100 - l) = 60/40$, so $l = 60$ cm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a metre bridge, an unknown X in the left gap balances a 10 Ω resistor in the right gap at 50.0 cm. A further 10 Ω resistor is then connected in series with X. The new balance point is about
questions.solution_md: First balance: $X = 10$ Ω. Now the left gap has 20 Ω: $\dfrac{20}{10} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$, so $l = 200/3 \approx 66.7$ cm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω and R = 15 Ω. Find the value of S, in ohms, for which the galvanometer shows no deflection.
questions.solution_md: Balance: $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$, so $S = \dfrac{RQ}{P} = \dfrac{15 \times 20}{10} = 30$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: In a metre bridge with an unknown resistance X in the left gap and 6.0 Ω in the right gap, the balance point is 60.0 cm from the left end. Find X, in ohms.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$: $X = 6.0 \times \dfrac{60}{40} = 9$ Ω.

options.text_md: becomes unbalanced, with current from B to D
becomes unbalanced, with current from D to B

questions.solution_md: The balance condition $P/Q = R/S$ does not involve the emf; all potentials scale together, so B and D stay at equal potential — option (b).

options.text_md: becomes non-zero, because current now flows through the 5 Ω resistor

questions.solution_md: At balance B and D are at the same potential, so no current flows through anything joined between them; nothing changes — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A balanced Wheatstone bridge stays balanced if the cell and the galvanometer are interchanged.

**Reason (R):** At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A follows because the balance condition $P/Q = R/S$ is the same as $P/R = Q/S$, the condition for the interchanged arrangement — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why is it best to choose the known resistance in a metre bridge experiment so that the balance point is near the middle of the wire?

The **end resistances** (contacts and copper strips) are also small compared with the resistance of each part of the wire. So the result is most accurate.

questions.solution_md: Consider percentage errors in l and 100 − l and end resistances.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define drift velocity and relaxation time. (b) Derive the expression for the drift velocity of electrons in terms of the applied field. (c) Use it to show that the resistivity of a metal is $\rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$. (d) Find the drift speed when 1.5 A flows through a copper wire of cross-section 1.0 mm² ($n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}$ m⁻³).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Drift velocity:** average velocity acquired by free electrons in a conductor due to an applied field. **Relaxation time** $\tau$: average time between successive collisions of an electron.

(b) Each electron has acceleration $\vec a = -e\vec E/m$. Just after a collision its velocity is random, $\vec v_0$, averaging to zero. After time $t_i$: $\vec v_i = \vec v_{0i} - \dfrac{e\vec E}{m}t_i$. Averaging over all electrons, the average of $t_i$ is $\tau$: $\vec v_d = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m}\tau$.

(c) $I = n e A v_d = n e A\dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ with $E = V/l$: $I = \dfrac{n e^2\tau A}{ml}V$. Comparing with $V = IR = I\rho\dfrac{l}{A}$ gives $\rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$.

(d) $v_d = \dfrac{I}{n e A} = \dfrac{1.5}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Average the velocities after collisions; then compare I = n e A v_d with Ohm’s law.

marking_scheme.step: Velocity after time t and averaging
ρ = m/(ne²τ) from I = n e A v_d

questions.stem_md: (a) Distinguish between the emf and the terminal voltage of a cell, and derive $V = E - Ir$. (b) Three cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.20 Ω, are used to drive current through a 6.0 Ω resistor. Find the current when the cells are joined (i) in series, (ii) in parallel. (c) Which arrangement gives the larger current here, and why?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **EMF** is the p.d. across the terminals when no current flows (the work done per unit charge by the cell). **Terminal voltage** is the p.d. across the terminals when current flows. With current $I$: $E = I(R + r)$, so $V = IR = E - Ir$: the "lost volts" $Ir$ are used inside the cell.

(b)(i) Series: emf $4.5$ V, internal resistance $0.60$ Ω: $I = \dfrac{4.5}{6.0 + 0.60} = 0.682$ A.
(ii) Parallel: emf $1.5$ V, internal resistance $0.20/3$ Ω: $I = \dfrac{1.5}{6.0 + 0.0667} \approx 0.247$ A.

(c) **Series** gives about three times the current, because the external resistance (6.0 Ω) is much larger than the internal resistance (0.20 Ω): adding emfs matters more than reducing internal resistance.

questions.solution_md: Combine the cells first, then I = E_eq/(R + r_eq).

marking_scheme.step: EMF vs terminal voltage, V = E − Ir

questions.stem_md: (a) State Kirchhoff’s rules. (b) Two branches are connected between points A and B: branch 1 has an 8.0 V cell and a 2.0 Ω resistor, branch 2 has a 4.0 V cell and a 4.0 Ω resistor (both cells with their positive terminals towards A, negligible internal resistance), and a third branch is a 4.0 Ω resistor. Find the current in each branch and the potential difference between A and B. State which cell, if any, is being charged.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Junction rule:** the sum of currents into a junction equals the sum out (charge conservation). **Loop rule:** the algebraic sum of potential changes round any closed loop is zero (energy conservation).

(b) Let $I_1$ and $I_2$ flow up through the cell branches into A and $I_3$ flow from A to B through the 4.0 Ω resistor. Junction A: $I_1 + I_2 = I_3$.
Loop 1: $8.0 - 2.0I_1 - 4.0I_3 = 0$. Loop 2: $4.0 - 4.0I_2 - 4.0I_3 = 0$.
Solving: $I_1 = 1.50$ A, $I_2 = -0.25$ A, $I_3 = 1.25$ A, and $V_A - V_B = 4.0I_3 = 5.00$ V.
$I_2$ is negative, so 0.25 A flows down through the 4.0 V cell, entering at its positive terminal: the **4.0 V cell is being charged**.

questions.solution_md: Junction rule at A, then two independent loops.

marking_scheme.step: Currents I₁ = 1.5 A, I₂ = −0.25 A, I₃ = 1.25 A
V_AB = 5.0 V and the 4.0 V cell is charged

questions.stem_md: (a) Using Kirchhoff’s rules, derive the condition for balance of a Wheatstone bridge. (b) Describe how a metre bridge uses this principle. (c) With a 5.0 Ω resistor in the right gap of a metre bridge, the balance point is 37.5 cm from the left end. Find the unknown resistance in the left gap and the new balance point if the two resistors are interchanged.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Arms: P (A–B), Q (B–C), R (A–D), S (D–C); galvanometer B–D; cell across A–C. At balance $I_g = 0$, so the current $I_1$ in P also flows through Q, and $I_2$ in R also flows through S. Loop ABDA: $-I_1P + I_2R = 0$. Loop BCDB: $-I_1Q + I_2S = 0$. Dividing: $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.

(b) In a metre bridge, P and Q are the unknown X and a known R in two gaps, and the other two arms are the lengths $l$ and $100 - l$ of a uniform wire, whose resistances are proportional to length. A jockey is slid along the wire until the galvanometer reads zero: $\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$.

(c) $X = 5.0 \times \dfrac{37.5}{62.5} = 3.0$ Ω. After interchanging, $\dfrac{R}{X} = \dfrac{l'}{100 - l'}$, so $l' = 62.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Zero galvanometer current; two loops; divide. Then X/R = l/(100 − l).

marking_scheme.step: Currents at balance (same I₁ in P and Q, I₂ in R and S)
X = 3.0 Ω and new balance at 62.5 cm

questions.stem_md: (a) Sketch and explain how the resistivity of (i) a metal, (ii) an alloy such as nichrome, (iii) a semiconductor varies with temperature. (b) A silver wire has resistance 2.5 Ω at 27 °C. Its temperature coefficient of resistivity is 4.3 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. At what temperature is its resistance 2.7 Ω? (c) Why is a metal resistance thermometer possible but a nichrome one is not practical?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a)(i) **Metal:** $\rho$ rises almost linearly, $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$ — ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, $\tau$ falls. (ii) **Nichrome:** high $\rho$ that changes very little ($\alpha$ about ten times smaller than copper’s). (iii) **Semiconductor:** $\rho$ falls steeply — the number of charge carriers rises sharply with temperature.

(b) $\dfrac{2.7}{2.5} - 1 = 0.08 = 4.3 \times 10^{-3}(T - 27)$, so $T - 27 \approx 18.6$ and $T \approx 45.6$ °C.

(c) A thermometer needs a resistance that changes **noticeably and predictably** with temperature. A metal such as platinum has a sizeable $\alpha$; nichrome’s resistance hardly changes, so temperature changes would be too small to measure.

questions.solution_md: Describe the three curves with reasons; then rearrange R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)].

questions.passage_md: A car battery has an emf of 12.6 V and an internal resistance of 0.020 Ω. When the driver turns the key, the starter motor draws about 150 A for a few seconds. The driver notices that the headlights, which were already on, dim sharply while the engine is being started.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) 9.6 V

**(b)** 450 W

The very large starter current causes a large "lost voltage" $Ir = 3.0$ V inside the battery, so the **terminal voltage falls** from about 12.6 V to 9.6 V. **(b)** $P = I^2r = 150^2 \times 0.020 = 450$ W.

**(c)** (i) Terminal voltage falls by Ir.
